query: Consider the following context: The recent perspective of multiprincipal element alloys (MPEAs), also known as high-entropy alloys (HEAs), has emerged as a very promising area for material design. Additive manufacturing (AM) strategies have also been noted to provide additional strength to HEA systems. In the selected dual-nanoprecipitation Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA system, an additional strength of approximately 300–400 MPa was achieved by adopting an additive manufacturing route as compared to its cast and wrought counterparts. However, the challenge of oxidation degradation always imposes a severe limitation for high-temperature applications in gas turbines, power plants, and aerospace components. Hence, ensuring material sustainability, longevity, and integrity for high-temperature applications inevitably requires the exploration of the oxidation behavior of alloys. In that context, which method can be used for elucidating the mechanistic aspects and elemental redistribution of nanoprecipitates on oxidation behavior, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Performing atom probe tomography (APT) on Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA samples before and after controlled high-temperature oxidation will reveal that local elemental redistribution at nanoprecipitate–matrix interfaces largely governs the oxidation resistance and associated degradation mechanisms.
generation.material_initial_state: Dual-nanoprecipitation Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA fabricated via additive manufacturing.
generation.intervention: Expose the alloy to a high-temperature oxidizing environment that mimics gas turbine or aerospace service conditions, then prepare site-specific APT samples from the oxidized cross-sections for near-atomic-scale chemical analysis.
generation.conditions: Operate in air or controlled O2 partial pressure at temperatures relevant to gas turbine operation (e.g., 800–1000 °C) for set durations (e.g., 10–100 hours).
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoprecipitate interfaces where oxidation-induced elemental diffusion and phase transformations are most pronounced.
generation.mechanism: As oxidation proceeds, certain elements (e.g., Al) may migrate to form oxides, while others (e.g., Cr, Ti) may redistribute within the matrix. APT offers 3D compositional mapping at near-atomic resolution to elucidate these local diffusion pathways.
generation.predicted_outcome: APT data will show preferential oxidation of reactive elements and changes in local partitioning around the nanoprecipitates, leading to new or modified oxide scales and potentially influencing high-temperature mechanical properties.
generation.baseline: Oxidation behavior of cast or wrought Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA tested under similar conditions without APT-based characterization.
generation.boundary: Extended oxidation times or significantly higher temperatures than those tested could alter the relative stability of oxide phases and might require additional thermal cycling tests for broader validation.
generation.uncertainty: While we anticipate that APT reveals elemental gradients at nanoprecipitate interfaces, the exact oxide phase formation and precise thicknesses of distinct interfacial reaction layers remain uncertain without additional corroborative techniques (e.g., high-resolution electron microscopy).

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct controlled thermal oxidation on specimens for varying times (short and prolonged). Then prepare site-specific atom probe samples from regions near the oxide–metal interface.
measurements: High-resolution APT to map 3D elemental distributions near nanoprecipitates post-oxidation.
Complementary scanning/transmission electron microscopy of cross-sections to confirm oxide layer thickness and morphology.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If APT does not reveal any measurable elemental gradient or phase alteration near nanoprecipitates post-oxidation, the hypothesis linking local elemental redistribution at nanoprecipitate–matrix interfaces to oxidation resistance would be disproven.

cited_evidence.text: This paper utilizes in situ X-ray diffraction (XRD) to investigate the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy (HEA). We found that (1) Mn is the major oxide-forming element in both vacuum and air environments, leading to the formation of non-protective oxides that deplete the bulk alloy of Mn; (2) no oxides like Cr 2 O 3 , Fe 2 O 3 , or Fe 3 O 4 were observed during the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi, which contradicts some previous studies on the isothermal oxidation of CrMnFeCoNi HEA. We also analysed and compared the experimental results with thermodynamic calculations by using ThermoCalc version 2022b software following the CALPHAD method. ThermoCalc predicted spinel oxide in a vacuum environment, along with halite oxides observed in experimental results; also, in an atmospheric environment, it predicted only spinel, indicating the need for further investigation into factors to validate the thermodynamic predictions.
